analysis.one_liner: Legalizes importing lower-priced FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada for personal use and licensed pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Health Committee from January 2005 until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Americans bring up to a 90-day supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada across the border for personal use, and would let licensed pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers import drugs from Canada for dispensing in the U.S. To address safety concerns, it builds a large enforcement apparatus: licensing and registration for importers and internet pharmacies, import labels and tracking codes, detention and suspension powers for the FDA, anti-counterfeiting rules, and fees to pay for it all. It was introduced by Senator Judd Gregg with five Republican cosponsors and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs and could buy the same FDA-approved medicines more cheaply from Canadian pharmacies, plus licensed pharmacies and internet pharmacies that would gain a legal importation channel.

how_it_helps.text: Allows any individual to import an FDA-approved prescription drug from Canada for personal use, up to a 90-day supply, when purchased from a licensed Canadian pharmacy and accompanied by a valid prescription [S3].
Lets licensed U.S. pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers import prescription drugs from Canada for dispensing to U.S. patients, creating a legal channel for lower-priced medicines [S3].

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to give high priority to improving FDA information systems to detect intentionally adulterated prescription drugs, aiming to make the importation channel safe rather than merely open [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose revenue as patients and pharmacies buy the same drugs at Canadian prices; FDA, payment networks, and internet/advertising companies bear compliance costs funded by new user fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers; payment and ad companies

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes many of the most expensive drugs from importation entirely, including biological products, biotechnology-derived drugs such as monoclonal antibodies, drugs requiring refrigeration, intravenously injected drugs, and controlled substances [S3].

Personal importation is tightly limited: the drug must be carried on the person, capped at a 90-day supply, and accompanied by a prescription co-signed by a Canadian physician, making the individual route cumbersome compared with the pharmacy route [S3].

The bill imposes new compliance duties and liability on internet service and advertising providers that accept ads from unlicensed pharmacies, and requires credit card networks and banks to build systems to block payments to unlicensed internet pharmacies, costs that could be passed on broadly [S3].

Opponents of drug importation have long argued it risks counterfeit or adulterated medicines entering the U.S. supply; this bill responds with extensive inspection, labeling, and suspension powers, but the machinery adds cost and delay and depends on FDA capacity that critics said was inadequate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for patients is real: legal access to the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian prices for common non-biologic medicines. But the bill's own design limits how far that benefit reaches, since it excludes biologics and other high-cost drug categories and makes individual importation procedurally burdensome. The extensive safety machinery is a fair response to genuine counterfeit-drug risks, though it would mean new fees and compliance costs. On balance the bill favors consumers over the pharmaceutical industry, with the safety trade-off managed rather than ignored.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Judd Gregg introduced the Safe IMPORT Act on January 26, 2005, with five Republican cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on January 26, 2005 [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in committee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers were better off, since no legal importation channel opened and U.S. patients kept paying American prices; patients who might have bought cheaper Canadian drugs gained nothing.

for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire, bill sponsor

for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Smith, Collins, Coleman, Murkowski, and one other)

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed importation legislation, arguing it would undermine drug safety and their U.S. pricing

sides.party_line_note: All six senators behind the bill were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how the chamber would have split; pharmaceutical makers' opposition to importation was widely reported at the time.

industries.note: Legal importation from Canada would let patients and pharmacies buy the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into U.S. sales revenue. The industry historically fought importation bills, which died repeatedly without floor votes.

industries.industry: Licensed pharmacies and Canadian internet pharmacies
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, licensed channel for importing and dispensing lower-priced drugs, rewarding pharmacies that comply with the new registration, labeling, and licensing rules.

industries.industry: Credit card networks and payment processors
industries.note: The bill requires regulators to force payment systems to identify and block transactions with unlicensed internet pharmacies, adding compliance costs while supporting a consumer-safety goal.
Providers become liable for accepting ads from unlicensed pharmacies or ads claiming no prescription is needed, adding legal exposure while targeting the online gray market that harms patients.
